Clinical percentiles are presented for the subscales based on data from Carpenter et al. (2020) collected from N = 1,787 clinical outpatients presenting for treatment across a range of diagnoses. A percentile of 50 means the client has scored at the average level compared with the clinical group for that score.

Traditionally, a positive screen on the MDQ requires endorsement of 7 or more of 13 symptom items, multiple symptoms occurring at the same time, and symptoms causing notable psychosocial impairment (Hirschfeld et al., 2000). Under these conditions, the original validation study reported good sensitivity (73%) and very good specificity (90%) for bipolar disorder diagnosis. However, subsequent research has produced variable results depending on the clinical setting and population. A recent meta-analysis (Arbona-Lampaya et al., 2024) of 21 studies found that at the standard cutoff of 7 or more symptoms, summary sensitivity was .62 and summary specificity was .85 when pooled across studies. Sensitivity was notably higher when comparing bipolar disorder to unipolar depression (.76) but significantly reduced (.37) in studies excluding patients with known bipolar disorder, suggesting the MDQ performs best as a screening tool among mood disorder patients rather than as a general population case-finding instrument.

Clinical percentiles are presented for the two subscales as developed by Carpenter et al. (2020) on over 1,700 outpatients presenting for treatment across a range of diagnoses. A percentile of 50 means that the client has scored at the average level compared with the clinical group for that subscale.

source_guidance.title: MDQ Scoring & Interpretation
source_guidance.text: A total score is calculated for questions 1-13 and reported as a raw score and the percentage of items endorsed (raw score / number of items multiplied by 100), to provide an indication of the proportion of symptoms the respondent identified with.

source_guidance.title: MDQ Subscale Scores
source_guidance.text:
Subscale scores are also reported using 10 of the 13 symptom items:
Positive Activation (items 3, 4, 8, 9): assesses increased energy/activity, grandiosity, and decreased need for sleep. Individuals endorsing symptoms defining Positive Activation are not likely to report significant levels of negative affect and are likely to be energetic and extraverted. Individuals scoring high on Positive Activation may be less likely to rate their symptoms as impairing given that increased levels of energy and activity may be experienced as advantageous to some degree, especially if they are mild in nature. This factor is strongly associated with a bipolar disorder diagnosis.
Negative Activation (items 1, 2, 6, 7, 12, 13): assesses irritability, racing thoughts, levels of negative affectivity, and distractibility. This factor is strongly associated with bipolar disorder as well as a range of other disorders, many of them (e.g. depressive disorders, PDs, PTSD, GAD, substance use disorders) characterised by emotion dysregulation and/or transdiagnostic personality traits such as neuroticism and disinhibition. Clients high in Negative Activation may be at risk for engaging in impulsive behaviour in emotional situations.
Three items (5, 10, and 11) loaded highly onto both Positive and Negative Activation factors and were removed from the subscale model.

A total score is calculated for questions 1-13 and reported as a raw score and the percentage of
items endorsed (raw score / number of items multiplied by 100), to provide an indication of the
proportion of symptoms the respondent identified with.
MDQ Screening Criteria
In order to meet the threshold for positive screening regarding bipolar disorder, the scoring
method is as follows:
- A score of 7 or more for questions 1-13 (53% of items endorsed)
AND
- "Yes" to item 14 asking if the symptoms clustered in the same time period
AND
- Symptoms caused either "Moderate" or "Serious" problems (item 15).
MDQ Subscale Scores
Subscale scores are also reported using 10 of the 13 symptom items:
- Positive Activation (items 3, 4, 8, 9): assesses increased energy/activity, grandiosity, and
decreased need for sleep. Individuals endorsing symptoms defining Positive Activation are not
likely to report significant levels of negative affect and are likely to be energetic and extraverted.
Individuals scoring high on Positive Activation may be less likely to rate their symptoms as
impairing given that increased levels of energy and activity may be experienced as
advantageous to some degree, especially if they are mild in nature. This factor is strongly
associated with a bipolar disorder diagnosis.
- Negative Activation (items 1, 2, 6, 7, 12, 13): assesses irritability, racing thoughts, levels of

well as a range of other disorders, many of them (e.g. depressive disorders, PDs, PTSD, GAD,
substance use disorders) characterised by emotion dysregulation and/or transdiagnostic
personality traits such as neuroticism and disinhibition. Clients high in Negative Activation may
be at risk for engaging in impulsive behaviour in emotional situations.

assessments.title: Maladaptive Schema Scale – Young Schema Aligned (MSS-YSQ)

assessment.name: Maladaptive Schema Scale – Young Schema Aligned (MSS-YSQ)
assessment.description: The Maladaptive Schema Scale – Young Schema Aligned (MSS-YSQ) assesses maladaptive patterns of thoughts, behaviours and emotions. The MSS-YSQ is aligned with the the schemas defined in the Young Schema Questionnaire (YSQ) in 1990, but is shorter (76 questions) and uses contemporary psychometric techniques.

administration.instructions: This assessment will take about 8 minutes to complete. Below are statements that you might agree or disagree with. Please read each statement and indicate your level of agreement. Try not to spend too much time on a single question or be overly factual in your responses, rather base your answers on what you intuitively feel.

source_rule_excerpts: The Maladaptive Schema Scale – Young Schema Aligned – Dynamic (MSS-YSQ-Dynamic) is an adaptive version of the MSS-YSQ. The MSS-YSQ-Dynamic was developed by NovoPsych to reduce respondent burden and make comprehensive schema assessment more feasible in time-constrained clinical settings. The adaptive algorithm stops administering items when early responses indicate that further items are unlikely to provide additional clinically relevant information, while preserving complete assessment for potential or actual schema elevations. This reduces the number of items administered by 36%, on average, without compromising the identification of clinically relevant maladaptive schemas.
Scores for the 19 subscales are presented as an average score, where the number represents the level of agreement with the schema, as defined by the Likert scale:

A schema is considered to be moderate when an average score is 2.5 or more, while the schema is considered to be strong and of clinical significance when higher than the 90th percentile. Scores on the 90th percentile or higher indicate that the respondent scored in the top 10% compared with other patients receiving mental health care. The 90th percentile threshold varies across schemas between an average score of 2.75 (e.g Dependence) to 3.25 (e.g. Mistrust). A higher threshold for “strong” indicates that there is a higher prevalence of a “moderate” schema among mental health clients.

source_guidance.title: MSS-YSQ Scoring & Interpretation
source_guidance.text:
Scores for the 19 subscales are presented as an average score, where the number represents the level of agreement with the schema, as defined by the Likert scale:
Strongly Disagree = 0 Disagree = 1 Neutral = 2 Agree = 3 Strongly Agree = 4
Higher scores are indicative of stronger agreement with maladaptive schemas and are hypothesised to be associated with psychopathology and more dysfunctional relational, emotional or personal functioning.

A schema is considered to be moderate when an average score is 2.5 or more, while the schema is considered to be strong and of clinical significance when higher than the 90th percentile. Scores on the 90th percentile or higher indicate that the respondent scored in the top 10% compared with other patients receiving mental health care. The 90th percentile threshold varies across schemas between an average score of 2.75 (e.g Dependence) to 3.25 (e.g. Mistrust). A higher threshold for “strong” indicates that there is a higher prevalence of a “moderate” schema among mental health clients.
A strong schema represents broad agreement with the schemas that are of theoretical importance to schema therapy in addition to a score that deviates from typical patterns of responding.
Maladaptive Schemas with Strong Agreement / Percentage in Agreement
Scores are also presented as the percentage of responses where the client “Agreed” or “Strongly Agreed” with the items in the subscale, producing a “Percent in Agreement” metric.

Childhood Unmet Needs Schema Clusters

In addition, scores are presented for each of the six early childhood needs. High scores on a need cluster strongly suggest that the cause of the schema is rooted in early childhood experiences. Scores of 2 or above are considered clinically meaningful and are suggestive of a childhood need that was chronically disrupted.

assessment.name: Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness – Version 2 (MAIA-2)
assessment.description: The Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness – Version 2 (MAIA-2; Mehling et al., 2018) is a 37-item adult self-report measure that assesses interoceptive awareness, or how individuals perceive, interpret, and respond to internal bodily sensations. It captures multiple dimensions of body awareness, including the ability to attend to bodily signals, regulate emotions through bodily awareness, and either engage with or avoid physical sensations. source_rule_excerpts: Each item is rated from 0 (Never) to 5 (Always), with some items reverse-scored. Scoring consists of calculating the average score for each of the eight subscales (sum of responses to the items in the subscale divided by the number of items, then rounded to 2 decimal places). The resulting subscale score ranges from 0 to 5, where higher scores indicate greater interoceptive awareness in that dimension.
Results are presented in a summary table reporting each subscale average score and corresponding community percentile.

Each MAIA-2 subscale average score is converted to a community percentile, indicating how a respondent’s score compares with the general population. A percentile of 50 means the respondent scored at the community sample average on that subscale, while a percentile of 75 means they scored higher than 75% of the community sample. Percentiles are interpreted as follows: low (below the 25th percentile), average (25th to 75th percentile), and high (above the 75th percentile).

Scores within the average range indicate that the respondent’s interoceptive awareness on that facet is broadly comparable to the general population and is unlikely to require specific clinical attention. The MAIA-2 is most clinically informative at the extremes of the distribution, where scores fall outside the average range. Low scores may point to reduced body awareness or avoidant patterns that are relevant to case formulation, while high scores may reflect strengths that can be leveraged therapeutically, or in some profiles, heightened sensitivity that warrants further exploration.

For single administrations, a horizontal chart displays each subscale’s community sample percentile along a 0–100 axis, with shaded regions below the 25th and above the 75th percentile highlighting scores outside the average range. This provides a visual profile of interoceptive awareness relative to the normative sample.

For multiple administrations, each subscale is presented as a separate line graph plotting average scores over time. These allow clinicians to observe changes in each and monitor progress during treatment.

Percentile rankings for each MAIA-2 subscale are derived from the community normative sample reported in Mehling et al. (2018), comprising 1,090 adults (mean age 30.6 years, SD = 11.3). Percentiles are calculated from the reported mean and standard deviation for each subscale, under the assumption of an approximately normal distribution. A percentile of 50 indicates a score at the community sample average.

source_guidance.title: Scoring the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness – Version 2 (MAIA-2)
source_guidance.text:
Each item is rated from 0 (Never) to 5 (Always), with some items reverse-scored. Scoring consists of calculating the average score for each of the eight subscales (sum of responses to the items in the subscale divided by the number of items, then rounded to 2 decimal places). The resulting subscale score ranges from 0 to 5, where higher scores indicate greater interoceptive awareness in that dimension.
There is no total score calculated as higher scores do not uniformly indicate better outcomes across all subscales, and the pattern of scores across the profile is often more clinically informative than any individual subscale score. For example, elevated Noticing combined with low Not-Worrying may reflect distress rather than adaptive awareness. A total score would collapse these clinically important distinctions into a single number.

source_guidance.title: Interpreting MAIA-2 Subscales
source_guidance.text:
For all MAIA-2 subscales, higher scores indicate greater interoceptive awareness, generally reflecting adaptive capacities. Items marked (R) are reverse-scored. Low scores may be particularly clinically informative, as they can indicate reduced body awareness, avoidant coping, or a disrupted relationship with bodily experience.
While higher scores generally reflect more adaptive interoceptive functioning, scores should be interpreted in the context of the full subscale profile. The pattern of scores across subscales is often more clinically informative than any individual score considered in isolation.
1. Noticing (Items 1, 2, 3, 4) : Awareness of uncomfortable, comfortable, and neutral body sensations. A low score suggests the individual may have limited conscious awareness of what is happening in their body, potentially resulting in difficulties recognising early signs of stress, fatigue, or emotional shifts. A high score may indicate strong sensory awareness of bodily states, though in some individuals this may co-occur with heightened vigilance to physical sensations.
2. Not-Distracting (Items 5(R), 6(R), 7(R), 8(R), 9(R), 10(R)) : Tendency not to ignore or distract from sensations of pain or discomfort. A low score suggests the individual may tend to suppress or avoid uncomfortable body signals rather than attending to them, which may limit their capacity to use bodily information adaptively. A high score indicates a willingness to stay present with discomfort rather than turning away from it.
3. Not-Worrying (Items 11(R), 12(R), 13, 14, 15(R)) : Tendency not to worry or experience emotional distress with sensations of pain or discomfort. A low score suggests the individual may become emotionally distressed when they notice uncomfortable physical sensations, potentially amplifying pain or anxiety through worry. A high score indicates the ability to notice discomfort without it triggering an escalating emotional response.
4. Attention Regulation (Items 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22) : Ability to sustain and control attention to body sensations. A low score suggests difficulty deliberately directing, holding, or shifting attention to bodily signals, which may limit the use of body-based coping strategies. A high score indicates the individual can intentionally focus on, broaden, or redirect their bodily attention as needed.
5. Emotional Awareness (Items 23, 24, 25, 26, 27) : Awareness of the connection between body sensations and emotional states. A low score suggests the individual may have difficulty recognising how emotions manifest physically, which may present as alexithymia or difficulty labelling emotional states. A high score indicates strong awareness that body sensations and emotions are connected, though in some presentations this may be accompanied by heightened sensitivity to the physical aspects of anxiety.
6. Self-Regulation (Items 28, 29, 30, 31) : Ability to regulate psychological distress by attending to body sensations. A low score suggests the individual may not use body awareness as a tool for managing distress, for example, using breath to reduce tension or calm down, and may represent a useful target for therapeutic intervention. A high score indicates the individual may actively draw on bodily attention to regulate their emotional state.
7. Body Listening (Items 32, 33, 34) : Active listening to the body for insight and decision-making. A low score suggests the individual may not generally consult their body for information when making decisions or trying to understand how they feel. A high score indicates they may actively seek out and use bodily signals to guide their responses and choices.
8. Trusting (Items 35, 36, 37) : Experience of one’s body as safe and trustworthy. A low score suggests the individual may not feel at home in their body, or may experience their body as unreliable or threatening. This may be particularly relevant in trauma, chronic pain, and depersonalisation presentations. A high score indicates a felt sense of safety and reliability in one’s bodily experience.

source_guidance.title: MAIA-2 Percentiles
source_guidance.text:
Each MAIA-2 subscale average score is converted to a community percentile, indicating how a respondent’s score compares with the general population. A percentile of 50 means the respondent scored at the community sample average on that subscale, while a percentile of 75 means they scored higher than 75% of the community sample. Percentiles are interpreted as follows: low (below the 25th percentile), average (25th to 75th percentile), and high (above the 75th percentile).
Scores within the average range indicate that the respondent’s interoceptive awareness on that facet is broadly comparable to the general population and is unlikely to require specific clinical attention. The MAIA-2 is most clinically informative at the extremes of the distribution, where scores fall outside the average range. Low scores may point to reduced body awareness or avoidant patterns that are relevant to case formulation, while high scores may reflect strengths that can be leveraged therapeutically, or in some profiles, heightened sensitivity that warrants further exploration.

source_guidance.title: Normative Data and Percentile Rankings of the MAIA-2
source_guidance.text:
Percentile rankings for each MAIA-2 subscale are derived from the community normative sample reported in Mehling et al. (2018), comprising 1,090 adults (mean age 30.6 years, SD = 11.3). Percentiles are calculated from the reported mean and standard deviation for each subscale, under the assumption of an approximately normal distribution. A percentile of 50 indicates a score at the community sample average.
Normative (community sample) means and standard deviations for MAIA-2 subscales (Mehling et al., 2018):
1. Noticing : M = 3.34, SD = 0.90
2. Not-Distracting : M = 2.06, SD = 0.80
3. Not-Worrying : M = 2.52, SD = 0.85
4. Attention Regulation : M = 2.84, SD = 0.86
5. Emotional Awareness : M = 3.44, SD = 0.96
6. Self-Regulation : M = 2.78, SD = 1.01
7. Body Listening : M = 2.20, SD = 1.17
8. Trusting : M = 3.37, SD = 1.11

source_guidance.title: Is there a total score?
source_guidance.text: No. The eight MAIA-2 subscales measure distinct aspects of interoceptive awareness that can vary independently within the same individual. For example, a person may score high on Noticing (strong awareness of body sensations) but low on Not-Worrying (tendency to become distressed by those sensations). Combining these into a single score would obscure clinically meaningful variation. Each subscale should be interpreted individually, with particular attention to the overall profile pattern. Subscales flagged as low (below 25th percentile) or high (above 75th percentile) relative to the community sample are most likely to inform case formulation and treatment planning. The pattern of scores across subscales can also be informative. For instance, elevated scores on awareness-related subscales (such as Noticing, Emotional Awareness, or Body Listening) combined with low scores on regulatory or tolerance subscales (such as Not-Distracting, Not-Worrying, or Trusting) may suggest that body awareness is experienced as distressing rather than adaptive. Clinicians should consider both individual subscale scores and the relationships between them when interpreting results.

A percentile of 50 means the respondent scored at the community sample average on that subscale, while a percentile of 75 means they scored higher than 75% of the community sample.
Percentiles are interpreted as follows: low (below the 25th percentile), average (25th to 75th percentile), and high (above the 75th percentile).
Percentile rankings for each MAIA-2 subscale are derived from the community normative sample reported in Mehling et al.
Percentiles are calculated from the reported mean and standard deviation for each subscale, under the assumption of an approximately normal distribution.
A percentile of 50 indicates a score at the community sample average.
Subscales flagged as low (below 25th percentile) or high (above 75th percentile) relative to the community sample are most likely to inform case formulation and treatment planning.

source_guidance.title: MAIA-Y Scoring & Interpretation
source_guidance.text:
The results from the MAIA-Y focuses upon the individual scale scores (between 0 and 5), where higher score equates to more awareness of bodily sensation. A percentile is also calculated, indicating how the responded scored in comparison to an age related normative sample. Interpretation using percentiles helps contextualise scores. For example, percentile below 50 indicate that the individual scored below what is typical. Extreme percentile scores (below 10 or above 90) are of particular clinical significance.
The MAIA consists of eight scales:
1. Noticing (Items 1-4): Awareness of uncomfortable, comfortable, and neutral body sensations
2. Not-Distracting (Items 5-7): Higher scores suggest a more tuned in relationship to unpleasant sensations, and is typically considered to be adaptive. Lower scores indicate the tendency to ignore or distract oneself from sensations of pain or discomfort
3. Not-Worrying (Items 8-10): Higher scores indicate less rumination about discomfort. Low scores indicate emotional distress or worry with sensations of pain or discomfort
4. Attention Regulation (Items 11-17): Ability to sustain and control attention to body sensation
5. Emotional Awareness (Items 18-22): Awareness of the connection between body sensations and emotional states
6. Self-Regulation (Items 23-26): Ability to regulate psychological distress by attention to body sensations
7. Body Listening (Items 27-29): Actively listens to the body for insight
8. Trust (Items 30-32): Experiences one’s body as safe and trustworthy

assessments.title: Multidimensional Inventory of Dissociation – 60-item Adolescent version (MID-60-A)

assessment.name: Multidimensional Inventory of Dissociation – 60-item Adolescent version (MID-60-A)
assessment.description: The Multidimensional Inventory of Dissociation 60-item – Adolescent version (MID-60-A) is a screening tool for adolescents (16-19 years) that assesses dissociative symptoms and experiences specific to DSM-5-TR dissociative disorders. It also captures dissociative experiences, PTSD and somatic symptoms, and phenomena closely related to dissociation such as trance and self-confusion. The MID-60-A is the adolescent version of the MID-60 used in adults, with minor changes to two questions (50 and 52).

source_guidance.title: MID-60-A Scoring & Interpretation
source_guidance.text:
A total mean score (range 0 to 100) is calculated by averaging all 60 responses and multiplying by 10. The mean score represents to total level of dissociative experiences, also interpreted as percentage of time the person self-reports having dissociative symptoms and experiences.
Two percentiles are presented for the total mean score, indicating how the respondent scored in comparison to normative and clinical populations.
The normative percentile provides a comparison against a sample of typical individuals (Kate et al., 2021). A percentile of 50 represents average (and healthy) levels of dissociative experiences. In contrast, a percentile of 90 indicates the respondent scored above 90 percent of typical individuals and is of clinical significance.
The clinical percentile compares the respondent’s score against people who have been diagnosed with a dissociative disorder (Kate, Jamieson & Middleton, 2021; 2022). A clinical percentile of 50 represents pathological levels of dissociation that is typical among those with a dissociative disorder.
Interpretation for the MID-60-A mean scores is as follows:
0–7: Does not have dissociative experiences
7–14: Has few diagnostically significant dissociative experiences
15–20: Mild dissociative symptoms and experiences. PTSD or a mild dissociative disorder (such as dissociative amnesia, depersonalisation / derealisation disorder) are possible
21–30: May have dissociative disorder and/or PTSD
31–40: May have a dissociative disorder (such as OSDD-1 or DID) and PTSD
41–64: Probably has DID or a severe dissociative disorder and PTSD
64 +: Severe dissociative and post-traumatic symptoms. High scores may also reflect neuroticism, attention seeking behaviour, exaggeration or malingering of symptoms, or psychosis
Subscales The MID-60-A provides information on subscales relevant to different diagnoses. This enables the clinician to form an impression about the likely diagnosis. For example, a score of 27 is clinically significant, but does not indicate the most likely diagnosis. If the subscales of PTSD and depersonalisation/derealisation are both above the clinical threshold, this can indicate the person has the dissociative subtype of PTSD, whereas if the memory-related subscales are above the clinical threshold this can indicate dissociative amnesia. Another example is a person who has a total mean score of 45, which would seem to indicate dissociative identity disorder. Yet, if the subscale score for amnesia (for recent events) is not elevated, this points towards a more severe case of other specified dissociative disorder.
The subscales are:
DID: Amnesia (for recent events) – items 42, 45, 48, 58. Clinical cutoff = 10
DID / OSDD-1: Subjective awareness of alter personalities and self-states – items 3, 36, 39, 49, 57. Clinical cutoff = 20
DID / OSDD-1: Angry intrusions – items 28, 33, 35, 46, 60. Clinical cutoff = 18
DID / OSDD-1: Persecutory intrusions – items 22, 37, 44, 56, 59. Clinical cutoff = 18
Derealisation/Depersonalisation – items 2, 7, 9, 13, 25, 47, 50, 53. Clinical cutoff = 20
Dissociative Amnesia: Distress about severe memory problems – items 1, 8, 20, 38, 43, 52. Clinical cutoff = 30
Dissociative Amnesia: Loss of autobiographical memory – items 16, 19, 24, 29, 34. Clinical cutoff = 34
PTSD: Flashbacks – items 4, 15, 31, 40, 54. Clinical cutoff = 16
Conversion Disorder: Body symptoms – items 5, 10, 14, 18. Clinical cutoff = 10
Conversion Disorder: Pseudo-Seizures (Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures) – item 26. Clinical cutoff = 10
General Subscales: Trance – items 21, 27, 30, 32, 41, 51. Clinical cutoff = 11.7
General Subscales: Self-confusion – items 6, 11, 12, 17, 23, 55. Clinical cutoff = 33.3
The MID-60-A is for screening purposes, is not designed to be the sole determinant of a diagnosis and should always be used in conjunction with clinical expertise. Further evaluations can be conducted with the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 Dissociative Disorders (SCID-D) or Dissociative Disorders Interview Schedule (DDIS).

assessment.name: Multidimensional Inventory of Dissociation – 60-item version (MID-60)
assessment.description: The Multidimensional Inventory of Dissociation 60-item version (MID-60) is a screening tool for adults (18 years +) that assesses dissociative symptoms and experiences consistent with DSM-5-TR dissociative disorders. It also captures dissociative experiences, PTSD and somatic symptoms, and phenomena closely related to dissociation such as trance and self-confusion. There is also an adolescent version for use with adolescents ages 16 to 19 years of age – the MID-60-A .

administration.instructions: How often do you have the following experiences when you are not under the influence of alcohol or drugs? Please select the number that best describes you. Select a “0” if the experience never happens to you; select a “10” if it is always happening to you. If it happens sometimes, but not all the time, choose a number between 1 and 9 that best describes how often it happens to you.

source_rule_excerpts: The MID-60 and DES-II both assess dissociation, but they differ in scope and sensitivity. The MID-60 replicates the 218-tem MID’s 12-factor structure, each with clinically meaningful cut-offs. This gives the MID-60 an important advantage over the DES-II, which was primarily designed to detect dissociative identity disorder and does this very well. However, the commonly recommended DES-II cut-off of 30 misses the majority of cases of dissociative amnesia, depersonalization/derealization disorder, and milder forms of other specified dissociative disorder (OSDD). As a result, the MID-60 is better suited to identifying a broader range of clinically significant dissociative presentations.

The MID-60 employs a 16-category diagnostic profile classification system based on a priori rules (Kate et al., 2026). Respondents are assigned to the first category for which criteria are met, evaluated hierarchically in descending order of clinical severity. The algorithm considers total MID-60 severity, specific subscale elevations at clinical cutoff, and symptom co-occurrence patterns.

Two percentiles are presented for the total mean score, indicating how the respondent scored in comparison to community and clinical populations. The community percentile provides a comparison against a sample of typical individuals (Kate et al., 2021). A percentile of 50 represents average (and healthy) levels of dissociative experiences. In contrast, a percentile of 90 indicates the respondent scored above 90 percent of typical individuals and is of clinical significance. The clinical percentile compares the respondent’s score against clients with a diagnosed dissociative disorder, comprising predominantly females with DID (Kate, Jamieson & Middleton, 2023). A clinical percentile of 50 represents pathological levels of dissociation that is typical among those with a complex dissociative disorder, particularly DID.

The MID-60 provides information on subscales relevant to different diagnoses. This enables the clinician to form an impression about the likely diagnosis. For example, a score of 27 is clinically significant, but does not indicate the most likely diagnosis. If the subscales of PTSD and depersonalisation/derealisation are both above the clinical threshold, this can indicate the person has the dissociative subtype of PTSD, whereas if the memory-related subscales are above the clinical threshold this can indicate dissociative amnesia. Another example is a person who has a total mean score of 45, which would seem to indicate dissociative identity disorder. Yet, if the subscale score for amnesia (for recent events) is not elevated, this points towards a more severe case of other specified dissociative disorder.

1. DID: Amnesia (for recent events) – items 42, 45, 48, 58. Clinical cutoff = 10. Assesses episodes of “losing time,” finding oneself in unexpected locations, discovering unexplained changes to appearance, and regaining awareness with objects in hand with no memory of how they got there

2. DID / OSDD-1: Subjective awareness of alter personalities and self-states – items 3, 36, 39, 49, 57. Clinical cutoff = 20. Subjective Awareness of Alter Personalities and Self-States: Evaluates awareness of distinct personality states or “parts” with their own identities, voices, and perspectives, including hearing child voices internally and sensing other people inside who can speak or take control

3. DID / OSDD-1: Angry intrusions – items 28, 33, 35, 46, 60. Clinical cutoff = 18. Measures intrusions of anger that feel outside one’s control, including words or actions not remembered after calming down

4. DID / OSDD-1: Persecutory intrusions – items 22, 37, 44, 56, 59. Clinical cutoff = 18. Assesses critical, hostile, or self-destructive internal voices that demean, command self-harm, or wish the individual dead

5. Derealisation/Depersonalisation – items 2, 7, 9, 13, 25, 47, 50, 53. Clinical cutoff = 20. Evaluates experiences of unreality about oneself, others, or surroundings, including feeling detached from one’s body or emotions and perceiving the world as foggy or distant

6. Dissociative Amnesia : Distress about severe memory problems – items 1, 8, 20, 38, 43, 52. Clinical cutoff = 30. Measures subjective distress related to pervasive memory difficulties affecting daily functioning

7. Dissociative Amnesia : Loss of autobiographical memory – items 16, 19, 24, 29, 34. Clinical cutoff = 34. Assesses substantial gaps in personal history, including missing periods from childhood or feeling that important life events cannot be recalled
8. PTSD: Flashbacks – items 4, 15, 31, 40, 54. Clinical cutoff = 16. Evaluates intrusive re-experiencing of traumatic memories with vivid sensory detail

9. Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder): Body symptoms – items 5, 10, 14, 18. Clinical cutoff = 10. Measures episodes of neurological symptoms without medical explanation, including temporary blindness, deafness, paralysis, or difficulty swallowing

10. Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder): Pseudo-Seizures (Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures) – item 26. Clinical cutoff = 10. Assesses seizure-like episodes that are not epileptic in origin

11. General Subscales: Trance – items 21, 27, 30, 32, 41, 51. Clinical cutoff = 11.7. Evaluates prolonged trance states characterised by staring, reduced awareness, and disconnection from present reality

12. General Subscales: Self-confusion – items 6, 11, 12, 17, 23, 55. Clinical cutoff = 33.3. Measures profound uncertainty about identity, including confusion about who one is and struggling to maintain a coherent sense of self

source_guidance.title: MID-60 Scoring & Interpretation
source_guidance.text: A total mean score (range 0 to 100) is calculated by averaging all 60 responses and multiplying by 10. The mean score represents the total level of dissociative experiences, also interpreted as the percentage of time the person self-reports having dissociative symptoms and experiences.

In contrast, a percentile of 90 indicates the respondent scored above 90 percent of typical individuals and is of clinical significance. source_guidance.title: MID-60 Total Score
source_guidance.text:
Interpretation for the MID-60 mean scores is as follows:
0–6: Does not have dissociative experiences
7–14: Has few diagnostically significant dissociative experiences
15–20: Mild dissociative symptoms and experiences. PTSD or a mild dissociative disorder (such as dissociative amnesia, depersonalisation / derealisation disorder) are possible
21–30: May have dissociative disorder and/or PTSD
31–40: May have a dissociative disorder (such as OSDD-1 or DID) and PTSD
41–63: Probably has DID or a severe dissociative disorder and PTSD
64–79: Severe dissociative and post-traumatic symptoms. Individuals with DID often score in this range. However, high scores may also reflect neuroticism, attention-seeking behaviour, exaggeration or malingering of symptoms, or psychosis
80+: Indicates an unusually high score, even among individuals diagnosed with severe and complex dissociative disorders

The subscales are:
1. DID: Amnesia (for recent events) – items 42, 45, 48, 58. Clinical cutoff = 10. Assesses episodes of “losing time,” finding oneself in unexpected locations, discovering unexplained changes to appearance, and regaining awareness with objects in hand with no memory of how they got there
2. DID / OSDD-1: Subjective awareness of alter personalities and self-states – items 3, 36, 39, 49, 57. Clinical cutoff = 20. Subjective Awareness of Alter Personalities and Self-States: Evaluates awareness of distinct personality states or “parts” with their own identities, voices, and perspectives, including hearing child voices internally and sensing other people inside who can speak or take control
3. DID / OSDD-1: Angry intrusions – items 28, 33, 35, 46, 60. Clinical cutoff = 18. Measures intrusions of anger that feel outside one’s control, including words or actions not remembered after calming down
4. DID / OSDD-1: Persecutory intrusions – items 22, 37, 44, 56, 59. Clinical cutoff = 18. Assesses critical, hostile, or self-destructive internal voices that demean, command self-harm, or wish the individual dead
5. Derealisation/Depersonalisation – items 2, 7, 9, 13, 25, 47, 50, 53. Clinical cutoff = 20. Evaluates experiences of unreality about oneself, others, or surroundings, including feeling detached from one’s body or emotions and perceiving the world as foggy or distant
6. Dissociative Amnesia : Distress about severe memory problems – items 1, 8, 20, 38, 43, 52. Clinical cutoff = 30. Measures subjective distress related to pervasive memory difficulties affecting daily functioning
7. Dissociative Amnesia : Loss of autobiographical memory – items 16, 19, 24, 29, 34. Clinical cutoff = 34. Assesses substantial gaps in personal history, including missing periods from childhood or feeling that important life events cannot be recalled
8. PTSD: Flashbacks – items 4, 15, 31, 40, 54. Clinical cutoff = 16. Evaluates intrusive re-experiencing of traumatic memories with vivid sensory detail
9. Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder): Body symptoms – items 5, 10, 14, 18. Clinical cutoff = 10. Measures episodes of neurological symptoms without medical explanation, including temporary blindness, deafness, paralysis, or difficulty swallowing
10. Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (Conversion Disorder): Pseudo-Seizures (Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures) – item 26. Clinical cutoff = 10. Assesses seizure-like episodes that are not epileptic in origin
11. General Subscales: Trance – items 21, 27, 30, 32, 41, 51. Clinical cutoff = 11.7. Evaluates prolonged trance states characterised by staring, reduced awareness, and disconnection from present reality
12. General Subscales: Self-confusion – items 6, 11, 12, 17, 23, 55. Clinical cutoff = 33.3. Measures profound uncertainty about identity, including confusion about who one is and struggling to maintain a coherent sense of self

sourceGuidance.title: MID-60 Scoring & Interpretation
sourceGuidance.text: A total mean score (range 0 to 100) is calculated by averaging all 60 responses and multiplying by 10. The mean score represents the total level of dissociative experiences, also interpreted as the percentage of time the person self-reports having dissociative symptoms and experiences.

sourceGuidance.title: MID-60 Percentiles
sourceGuidance.text: Two percentiles are presented for the total mean score, indicating how the respondent scored in comparison to community and clinical populations. The community percentile provides a comparison against a sample of typical individuals (Kate et al., 2021). A percentile of 50 represents average (and healthy) levels of dissociative experiences. In contrast, a percentile of 90 indicates the respondent scored above 90 percent of typical individuals and is of clinical significance. The clinical percentile compares the respondent’s score against clients with a diagnosed dissociative disorder, comprising predominantly females with DID (Kate, Jamieson & Middleton, 2023). A clinical percentile of 50 represents pathological levels of dissociation that is typical among those with a complex dissociative disorder, particularly DID.

sourceGuidance.title: MID-60 Total Score
sourceGuidance.text:
Interpretation for the MID-60 mean scores is as follows:
0–6: Does not have dissociative experiences
7–14: Has few diagnostically significant dissociative experiences
15–20: Mild dissociative symptoms and experiences. PTSD or a mild dissociative disorder (such as dissociative amnesia, depersonalisation / derealisation disorder) are possible
21–30: May have dissociative disorder and/or PTSD
31–40: May have a dissociative disorder (such as OSDD-1 or DID) and PTSD
41–63: Probably has DID or a severe dissociative disorder and PTSD
64–79: Severe dissociative and post-traumatic symptoms. Individuals with DID often score in this range. However, high scores may also reflect neuroticism, attention-seeking behaviour, exaggeration or malingering of symptoms, or psychosis
80+: Indicates an unusually high score, even among individuals diagnosed with severe and complex dissociative disorders

assessment.name: Multilevel Assessment of Psychopathology (MAPsy)
assessment.description: The MAPsy is a 154-item self-report questionnaire that screens for the symptoms of DSM-5 disorders and shows which symptoms are elevated through two lenses: 33 disorder scales, and 127 dimensions of an empirically derived hierarchy of psychopathology. Designed as a broad initial assessment, it helps clinicians identify which areas warrant further assessment.

source_rule_excerpts: This means a percentile compares the client with people who may have been experiencing mental health difficulties, rather than with the general population. A percentile around 50 means a typical level of psychopathology for that group, not an average level for the community.

This follows from how the thresholds are set. For the constructs of the hierarchy, a construct’s thresholds are the sums of its items’ thresholds, so a broad construct with many items needs more of its items at or above threshold before its score reaches the Elevated or Clinically Significant band than a narrow construct with few items does. This is by design: for a spectrum’s score to reach the Elevated or Clinically Significant band, the client must report symptoms at threshold level across a substantial share of the spectrum’s content, which is what an elevation on a broad dimension of psychopathology means. The hierarchy therefore registers severity at the level at which it is present, narrow problems on clusters and pervasive difficulties on subfactors and spectra.

For some disorders, correct identification comes only after a long delay, even among people who have sought professional help. In a survey of 600 people with bipolar disorder, 69 percent reported having been misdiagnosed; those misdiagnosed had consulted an average of four clinicians before receiving the correct diagnosis, and more than a third waited 10 years or more for an accurate diagnosis (Hirschfeld et al., 2003). An average of about three years between first professional contact and diagnosis has been reported for obsessive-compulsive disorder (Stengler et al., 2013) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (Nylander et al., 2013), and a median of 11 years or more between first clinical evaluation and diagnosis for adults with autism spectrum disorder (Fusar-Poli et al., 2022). A broad assessment early in a person’s contact with mental health services or professionals is one way to bring such presentations to attention sooner.

The MAPsy yields scores for nine spectra, two subspectra, 21 subfactors, and 95 clusters of the empirical hierarchy, and for 23 personality facets, six neurocognitive domains, and 33 DSM-5 disorder scales. A construct’s score is the sum of its constituent item scores. Higher scores indicate that the construct’s items were rated as more true, or more common, over the past year.

The reference sample is best described as a distress-enriched sample: most of its members were receiving mental health treatment and more than half reported very high psychological distress. Percentiles therefore describe the client’s standing relative to that population rather than the general community. A score at the 50th percentile is typical of that population and does not indicate an average level of psychopathology relative to the general community. A distress-enriched sample has the advantage that its percentiles discriminate among individuals across the full range of severity, including the high levels seen in clinical settings.

Item-level thresholds. The thresholds of the constructs of the empirical hierarchy, the personality facets, and the neurocognitive domains are sums of item-level thresholds set by clinical review. Each of the 154 items was assigned a first threshold, the lowest item score indicating a level of psychopathology that is of clinical interest, and a second threshold, the lowest item score indicating a clinically significant level. The thresholds were set in three stages. First, three raters independently selected thresholds for every item. The consensus for each item was then taken as the median of the three selections, or agreed through discussion with a fourth rater where selections were widely split. Finally, the consensus thresholds were reviewed against each item’s content, considering the DSM-5 criterion the item describes, where it describes one, and the raters’ judgement of how common the experience is in everyday life. The rationale for each item’s thresholds was recorded. Items describing experiences judged common in everyday life were given higher thresholds, and items describing safety-critical or under-reported experiences, such as suicidal behaviour and antagonistic conduct, lower thresholds. The reference sample did not determine the item thresholds; the proportion of the sample at or above each threshold was consulted only as context.

Disorder scale thresholds. The thresholds for the 33 DSM-5 disorder scales were instead anchored to the prevalence of each disorder in the general population, taken from the DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2013, 2022), the National Comorbidity Survey Replication (Kessler et al., 2005), and, for disorders these do not cover, other national surveys and published epidemiological studies, using 12-month prevalence where available and point or lifetime prevalence otherwise. Summed item thresholds would have made the proportion of respondents reaching a disorder scale’s thresholds depend on the number of items describing the disorder’s criteria, from two to 53, rather than on how common the disorder is. For each scale, the Elevated threshold was set at the score at or above which the proportion of the reference sample is closest to six times the disorder’s prevalence, and the Clinically Significant threshold at the score closest to four times, the multipliers allowing for the reference sample’s enrichment for psychological distress relative to the general population.

source_guidance.title: MAPsy Scoring
source_guidance.text:
The MAPsy yields scores for nine spectra, two subspectra, 21 subfactors, and 95 clusters of the empirical hierarchy, and for 23 personality facets, six neurocognitive domains, and 33 DSM-5 disorder scales. A construct’s score is the sum of its constituent item scores. Higher scores indicate that the construct’s items were rated as more true, or more common, over the past year.
The score itself is not displayed in the report: it is converted to a percentile and assigned a severity band, and the report presents those.

For the Antisocial Personality Disorder with Psychopathic Features scale, the items measuring Anxiousness and Withdrawal are reverse scored before summing, so that low anxiousness and low withdrawal contribute to the scale in the direction that defines the disorder.

source_guidance.title: MAPsy Percentiles
source_guidance.text:
Percentiles are the primary metric for presenting scores because they are comparable across constructs, regardless of the number of items, and are readily communicated to clients and other professionals. Each score is converted to a percentile against the distribution of scores on that construct in a reference sample drawn from Forbes et al.’s (2025) study. Percentiles can be based on the whole reference sample, All (respondents aged 16 years and over), or on one of two subsets of it, Youth (16 to 24 years) and Adult (25 years and over). The Youth or Adult sample is selected by default from the client’s age at administration, calculated from their date of birth, and the Adult sample is used when no date of birth is entered.
The reference sample is best described as a distress-enriched sample: most of its members were receiving mental health treatment and more than half reported very high psychological distress. Percentiles therefore describe the client’s standing relative to that population rather than the general community. A score at the 50th percentile is typical of that population and does not indicate an average level of psychopathology relative to the general community. A distress-enriched sample has the advantage that its percentiles discriminate among individuals across the full range of severity, including the high levels seen in clinical settings.
The percentile does not itself say whether a level of psychopathology is clinically significant; that judgement is carried by the severity band. The percentile instead shows how far the client’s level of psychopathology is from what is typical of the reference sample.

source_guidance.title: Why are the percentiles based on a mental health sample rather than the general community?
source_guidance.text:
The reference sample was recruited for research on mental health; most of its members were receiving treatment and more than half reported very high psychological distress. This composition suits the measure’s purpose. A measure used to decide whether a presentation warrants further assessment needs to discriminate among individuals across the full range of severity, and a sample in which high levels of distress are common represents that range more fully than a general community sample, in which most respondents score near the floor and few score in the range where clinical decisions are made.
This means a percentile compares the client with people who may have been experiencing mental health difficulties, rather than with the general population. A percentile around 50 means a typical level of psychopathology for that group, not an average level for the community.
This is why the severity bands, which are fixed to the score and do not change with the reference sample selected, carry the judgement of whether a level of psychopathology is of clinical interest or clinically significant. The percentile shows where the client sits among people who were, for the most part, receiving mental health treatment.

source_guidance.title: Why does the Harmful Substance Use spectrum sometimes show no score?
source_guidance.text: Because it is scored only for clients who report using a substance in the past year. Part-way through the questionnaire, the client is asked which substances they have used in the past year, from a checklist of seven classes. A client who selects one or more is then asked nine further items about substance use disorder symptoms and use in dangerous situations, and the Harmful Substance Use spectrum is scored from those items. A client who selects “None of the above” is not asked these items, so the spectrum and its clusters are shown in the report without a score, and the three checklist clusters (Alcohol use, Cannabis use, and Illicit and prescription substance use) are marked No.

sourceGuidance.title: MAPsy Scoring
sourceGuidance.text:
The MAPsy yields scores for nine spectra, two subspectra, 21 subfactors, and 95 clusters of the empirical hierarchy, and for 23 personality facets, six neurocognitive domains, and 33 DSM-5 disorder scales. A construct’s score is the sum of its constituent item scores. Higher scores indicate that the construct’s items were rated as more true, or more common, over the past year.
The score itself is not displayed in the report: it is converted to a percentile and assigned a severity band, and the report presents those.

For the Antisocial Personality Disorder with Psychopathic Features scale, the items measuring Anxiousness and Withdrawal are reverse scored before summing, so that low anxiousness and low withdrawal contribute to the scale in the direction that defines the disorder.

descriptions.spectrum:Detachment: Measures disengagement from social and emotional life, together with low mood: reduced interest and pleasure, hopelessness and diminished self-worth, withdrawal from relationships and social contact, and a muted or unexpressed emotional range. In this measure, the dimension also encompasses reduced interest in sexual and romantic relationships.
descriptions.spectrum:Eating Pathology: Assesses disturbances of eating and body image, including fear of weight gain, the influence of weight or shape on self-evaluation, restrictive eating, and distress associated with overeating.
descriptions.spectrum:Externalising: Measures behaviour and emotion directed outward against other people, rules, or norms — a broad spectrum spanning impulsive, reckless, or aggressive conduct, manipulation and self-interest, reduced concern for others, and outwardly directed anger.
descriptions.spectrum:Harmful Substance Use: Assesses the core features of problematic alcohol and other drug use, including craving, loss of control over use, tolerance and withdrawal, continued use despite harm, and use in dangerous situations.
descriptions.spectrum:Internalising: Represents the broad propensity to experience negative emotions turned inward. This wide-ranging spectrum spans low mood, worry and anxious arousal, fear-based avoidance, social withdrawal, and trauma-related distress with disturbed sleep.
descriptions.spectrum:Mania: Measures the dimension of elevated and expansive mood. In this measure, it is assessed through euphoric mood, heightened sociability and talkativeness, unrestrained emotional expression, and enjoyment of attention.
descriptions.spectrum:Neurodevelopmental and Cognitiv: Encompasses difficulties of neurodevelopment and cognition — a broad spectrum spanning social communication, attentional and sensory regulation, ritualised and inflexible behaviour, and problems with memory, attention, and everyday cognitive functioning.
descriptions.spectrum:Somatoform: Assesses the experience of physical symptoms and bodily concern — pain, palpitations and breathlessness, temperature sensations, unsteadiness and slowed thinking or movement — together with health anxiety and disturbances of sleep and eating.
descriptions.spectrum:Thought Disorder: Measures disruptions to the ordinary integration of perception, thought, and consciousness, spanning psychotic-like experiences and beliefs, dissociative experiences, and associated physical and behavioural changes.
descriptions.subspectrum:Cognitive Difficulties: Assesses problems with everyday cognitive functioning: attention and concentration, memory, word-finding, planning and decision-making, mental speed, and the capacity to manage everyday tasks, possessions, and living spaces.
descriptions.subspectrum:Neurodevelopmental: Captures traits and difficulties commonly associated with neurodevelopmental conditions: social communication difficulties, overactivity and pressured speech, sensory sensitivity, unusually intense interests, and ritualised or inflexible behaviour.
descriptions.subfactor:Antagonism: Measures self-interested and manipulative interpersonal behaviour, including deceit, entitlement, attention-seeking, and deliberately annoying others.
descriptions.subfactor:Antisocial Behaviour: Represents the dimension of aggressive and harmful conduct. In this measure, it is assessed through physical aggression towards people, animals, or property.
descriptions.subfactor:Callousness: Assesses reduced empathy and emotional responsiveness to others: indifference to others' feelings, lack of concern about causing hurt, and a sense of personal superiority or entitlement.
descriptions.subfactor:Disinhibition: Measures deficient restraint over behaviour: acting without regard for consequences, recklessness, carelessness, and feeling or acting out of control.
descriptions.subfactor:Externalised Negative Affect: Captures negative emotion directed outward at other people and circumstances: irritability, anger and verbal outbursts, resentment, mistrust of others, and blaming others for one's own difficulties.
descriptions.subfactor:Distress: Represents the core negative-affect dimension of internalising — a broad blend of low mood and diminished pleasure, worry and anxious arousal, emotional lability, guilt and negative self-evaluation, and suicidality.
descriptions.subfactor:Dysregulated Sleep and Trauma: Assesses post-traumatic distress together with disturbed sleep: distress and avoidance connected to a traumatic experience, and difficulty falling or staying asleep.
descriptions.subfactor:Fear: Measures the phobic aspects of anxiety: fear and avoidance cued by particular objects, situations, or concerns — public or enclosed spaces, social scrutiny, specific phobic stimuli, illness and dying, bodily appearance, and rejection or abandonment.
descriptions.subfactor:Social Withdrawal: Assesses behavioural disengagement from social life — avoidance of and discomfort in social situations, anxiety about public spaces or being away from home, and diminished interest in other people — alongside lowered mood and enjoyment.
descriptions.subfactor:Difficulties with Organisation: Assesses difficulty keeping one's possessions and living environment manageable: losing needed items, clutter that limits the use of living areas, difficulty discarding possessions, and needing help with everyday household tasks.
descriptions.subfactor:Forgetfulness: Measures changes in memory and familiar abilities: difficulty recalling recent events, declining ease with familiar skills, and trouble finding one's way in familiar places.
descriptions.subfactor:Neurocognitive Impairment: Assesses a broad range of cognitive difficulties spanning attention, concentration, multitasking, memory, word-finding, mental speed and effort, planning and decision-making, and independence in daily activities.
descriptions.subfactor:Altered Sensation and Attentio: Measures dysregulation of attention, activity, speech, and sensory experience: restlessness and overactivity, pressured or excessive speech, sensitivity to sensory input, and unusually intense interests.
descriptions.subfactor:Ritualised Behaviour: Assesses rigid and repetitive patterns of behaviour: insistence on sameness, perfectionism, and repetitive acts performed to manage intrusive thoughts or distress, or to prevent something bad from happening.
descriptions.subfactor:Social Communication Difficult: Measures difficulty understanding and using communication in social interaction: following what others mean, holding reciprocal conversations, responding when others make contact, reading and using non-verbal cues, and adapting behaviour to the social context.
descriptions.subfactor:Dysregulated Eating: Represents the dimension of disrupted eating patterns that present alongside other physical symptoms. In this measure, it is assessed through eating large amounts of food in the absence of hunger.
descriptions.subfactor:Dysregulated Sleep: Assesses disturbance of the sleep–wake cycle as a physical presentation: difficulty falling or staying asleep, and excessive daytime sleepiness despite adequate sleep.
descriptions.subfactor:Somatic Symptoms: Measures the experience of distressing bodily symptoms — pain and muscle tension, palpitations and breathlessness, temperature sensations, unsteadiness and slowed thinking or movement — together with anxiety about one's physical health.
descriptions.subfactor:Dissociative Experiences: Assesses disruptions to the ordinary integration of consciousness, perception, memory, and identity: detachment from oneself or one's surroundings, gaps in memory, experiences of separate self-states, and sudden losses of control over thought, emotion, or behaviour.
descriptions.subfactor:Positive Psychosis: Measures psychotic-like experiences and beliefs: perceptions that others do not share, beliefs held despite contrary evidence, experiences of thought interference, and thinking or behaviour that others find strange.
descriptions.subfactor:Uncontrollable Physical Sympto: Assesses involuntary movements and unusual bodily sensations: trembling, chills, numbness or tingling, unsteadiness, and a sense of being slowed. In this measure, the dimension also encompasses being seen by others as odd or unusual.

assessment.name: NovoPsych Five Factor Personality Scale – 30 item version (NFFPS-30)
assessment.description: The NovoPsych Five Factor Personality Scale – 30 is a brief self-report personality inventory measuring the well established five factor model of personality (a.k.a OCEAN). It is for use by older adolescents (ages 16+) and adults, where personality characteristics are compared to age and gender norms on the five factors of Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism.

Describe yourself as you honestly see yourself, in relation to other people you know of the same sex as you are, and roughly your same age.

source_guidance.title: NFFPS-30 Scoring & Interpretation
source_guidance.text:
The NFFPS-30 assesses an individual’s personality across five major factors, which are further divided into facets:
Openness to Experience: Measures receptiveness to new ideas, imagination, and intellectual curiosity.
Imagination: Assesses the inclination to engage in vivid imagination and daydreaming (Item 13).
Artistic Interests: Reflects the appreciation for art, beauty, and aesthetic experiences (Item 25).
Emotionality: Measures the openness and expression of emotions and emotional experiences (Item 26).
Adventurousness: Assesses the willingness to try new experiences and tolerance for change (Item 17).
Intellect: Reflects the openness to new ideas, intellectual curiosity, and interest in abstract thinking (Item 29).
Liberalism: The importance placed on ethical, philosophical, and moral principles as determined by political persuasion (Item 22).
Conscientiousness : Reflects how organised, responsible, and goal-oriented a person is.
Self-Efficacy: Reflects the belief in one’s own capabilities to successfully accomplish tasks and goals (Item 24).
Orderliness: Measures the preference for structure, organisation, and tidiness in one’s environment (Item 15).
Dutifulness: Reflects the sense of responsibility, duty, and obligation towards fulfilling tasks and commitments (Item 27).
Achievement Striving: Assesses the drive for success, setting high personal standards, and working diligently towards goals (Item 18).
Self-Discipline: Reflects the ability to control impulses, maintain focus, and persevere in the face of challenges (Item 21).
Cautiousness: Measures the inclination to think carefully, consider alternatives, and approach decisions cautiously. This facet is not akin to risk aversion, but rather more in line with deliberate decision making (Item 8).
Extraversion : Measures the extent to which a person is outgoing, energetic, and sociable.
Friendliness: Assesses the inclination to be warm, affable, and friendly towards others (Item 12).
Gregariousness: Reflects the enjoyment of being in social situations and seeking out the company of others (Item 3).
Assertiveness: Measures the tendency to express opinions, desires, and needs confidently and directly (Item 4).
Activity Level: Assesses the preference for being active, energetic, and engaged in physical and mental pursuits (Item 6).
Excitement Seeking: Reflects the inclination to seek out novel, thrilling, and stimulating experiences (Item 19).
Cheerfulness: Measures the tendency to experience positive emotions, joyfulness, and optimism (Item 30).
Agreeableness : Assesses the level of compassion, cooperativeness, and kindness in an individual.
Trust: Reflects the tendency to believe in the sincerity and trustworthiness of others (Item 1).
Morality: Measures the importance placed on adhering to ethical principles concerning other people’s rights (Item 14).
Altruism: Assesses the extent to which a person is inclined to help and support others (Item 10).
Cooperation: Reflects the willingness to work harmoniously with others and avoid conflicts (Item 9).
Modesty: Measures the inclination to downplay one’s own achievements and avoid self-promotion (Item 20).
Sympathy: Assesses the ability to understand and feel compassion for others’ emotions and experiences (Item 7).
Neuroticism : Evaluates emotional stability, anxiety levels, and sensitivity to stress.
Anxiety: Assesses the tendency to experience worry, unease, and nervousness (Item 23).
Anger: Reflects the proneness to experience feelings of anger, irritation, and hostility (Item 2).
Depression: Measures the tendency to experience sadness, low mood, and feelings of hopelessness (Item 16).
Self-Consciousness: Assesses the level of self-awareness and concern about how one is perceived by others (Item 5).
Immoderation: Reflects the inclination to engage in excessive or impulsive behaviour (Item 28).
Vulnerability: Measures the sensitivity to stress, emotional reactivity, and susceptibility to negative emotions (Item 11).

These factors and facets provide a comprehensive assessment of an individual’s personality traits and help practitioners gain insights into various aspects of an individual’s behaviour and preferences.
Percentiles are presented for each of the trait factors and facets, comparing the respondent’s scores to those of an age and gender related Australian sample (NovoPsych’s analysis of Johnson 2020 data). A percentile of 50 represents typical patterns of responding compared to peers. Descriptors for each factor and facet are also presented where it is considered High if the score is in the top 30% compares to peers, Low if in the bottom 30% or Average if in the middle 40% (i.e., High if the percentile is 70 or above, Low if the percentile is 30 or below, or Average if the percentile is between 30 and 70). Percentiles are based upon gender and age, which was categorised into the seven age groups.
On a facet level, percentiles may be presented with > or < symbols. This indicates that the top (>) or bottom (<) percentile rank has been reached due to ceiling or floor effects for that facet. Given that facets are derived from single items, caution is recommended when interpreting facet scores.
In the narrative report, ‘pattern types’ may also be presented (if there are high and low scores on personality factors). These ‘pattern types’ are based on the Abridged Big Five-Dimensional Circumplex (AB5C; Hofstee, de Raad, & Goldberg, 1992) model of personality. These descriptions are based upon those provided by Johnson (n.d.).

assessments.title: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Child Self Report (ChOCI-R-S)

assessment.name: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Child Self Report (ChOCI-R-S)
assessment.description: The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) is a 38-item self-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by the child or adolescent and measures both the obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours they experience and the impairment these cause in daily life. There is also a parent-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-P ) that can be completed by a parent or caregiver.

administration.instructions: Each of the following questions asks you about things or “habits” you feel you have to do although you may know that they do not make sense. Sometimes, you may try to stop from doing them but this might not be possible. You might feel worried or angry or frustrated until you have finished what you have to do. An example of a habit like this may be the need to wash your hands over and over again even though they are not really dirty, or the need to count up to a special number (e.g. 6 or 10) while you do certain things. Please answer each question by indicating how much you agree with the statement, or how much you think it is true of you. Please answer each item, without spending too much time on any one item. There are no right or wrong answers. Compulsions· symptoms

scoring.coverage: Implemented formulas have explicit item membership and numeric source evidence. Remaining expressions, diagnostic algorithms, percentiles, custom missing-answer policies and interpretation require review.
source_rule_excerpts: Total Symptoms (sum of Compulsion Symptoms and Obsession Symptoms; scores range from 0 to 40) Compulsion Symptoms (items 1 to 10; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items Obsession Symptoms (items 20 to 29; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items

Total Impairment (sum of Compulsion Impairment and Obsession Impairment; scores range from 0 to 48) Compulsion Impairment (items 14 to 19; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items Obsession Impairment (items 33 to 38; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items

Each raw score is presented with a percentile rank against an OCD-clinical reference sample. A percentile of 50 corresponds to the OCD-clinical reference average; a percentile of 80 indicates a score exceeding approximately 80% of young people with OCD in the reference group. Because the norms come from an OCD-diagnosed sample, a low percentile does not mean a young person does not have OCD, only that their symptoms or impairment are milder than most others with the condition.

On first administration, the report presents a results table followed by two construct sections (Symptoms and Impairment). Each section contains two horizontal raw-score charts. The first plots the construct’s total as a single bar with the client’s raw score on a 0–40 axis for Symptoms or 0–48 for Impairment. A clinical 25th-to-75th percentile reference rectangle and a dashed line at the clinical average show the score relative to the clinical reference sample of young people with OCD. The second plots the construct’s two subscales (Compulsion and Obsession bars on a 0–20 axis for Symptoms or 0–24 for Impairment, each with its own 25th-to-75th reference rectangle and clinical-average line). Beneath each bar, a coloured strip marks that scale’s descriptor bands (Low, Moderate and High for Symptoms; Minimal, Mild, Moderate, Severe and Extreme for Impairment, with Minimal shown in white).

Reference percentiles are derived from Uher and colleagues (2008): 285 consecutive referrals (244 to 278 with complete self-report data per subscale) to an OCD clinic between 2000 and 2006, all meeting ICD-10 criteria for OCD via structured clinical interview, with no significant sex differences (boys’ age M = 13.7, range 7 to 18; girls’ age M = 13.7, range 9 to 18). Reference parameters for the self-report subscales are: Compulsion Symptoms M = 9.5, SD = 4.3; Obsession Symptoms M = 8.0, SD = 5.1; Total Symptoms M = 17.6, SD = 7.8; Compulsion Impairment M = 15.0, SD = 4.5; Obsession Impairment M = 13.5, SD = 5.2; Total Impairment M = 28.5, SD = 8.7. Because this reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed reference group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a young person diagnosed with OCD, not the general population. No community-sample reference data exists for the self-report ChOCI-R-S, and the original authors note that confirmation in primary care and population-based samples remains needed (Uher et al., 2008).

The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement. NovoPsych placed each subscale’s cut-offs at the same percentile as the matching Total cut-off, using each subscale’s own mean and SD from Uher et al. (2008), with each band starting at the next whole score. For symptoms, Moderate starts at about the 16th percentile and High at about the 84th. For impairment, Mild starts at about the 1st–2nd percentile, Moderate about the 16th, Severe about the 56th and Extreme about the 90th. The parent-report ChOCI-R-P has different raw-score cut-offs, because each form is converted through its own column of the equivalence table and its own norms, so the same raw score does not mean the same thing on the two forms.
